turns.text: Turn the clock back to 2014. What problem was Sequence-to-Sequence Learning actually trying to solve?

Earlier neural language systems often depended on task-specific pipelines and fixed windows. Encoder-decoder models offered a general way to map an input sequence of one length to an output sequence of another length.
That sounds like a promising direction. What mechanism actually makes it work?

An encoder reads the source sequence into a learned representation, and a decoder generates the target sequence token by token. Training maximizes the conditional probability of the output sequence given the input.
Why did the idea outlive one paper or experiment? What did later researchers actually inherit?

Experts generally treat sequence-to-sequence learning as the architecture that made end-to-end neural translation practical before attention and Transformers. It also generalized to summarization, dialogue, parsing, and other structured generation tasks.
Sequence-to-Sequence Learning mattered not only as a result, but as a method that later researchers could test, adapt, and extend.
